steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on getting smaller open-source language models to self-refine their responses using external proxy metrics as feedback, applied to grounded question answering and dialogue data generation. Cover prior work on critique and refinement, the method, and the contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- LLMs for synthetic data; critique and refinement in prior work
- Self-refinement and its shortcomings; principles
- Our method: ProMiSe
- Applications and fine-tuning results
- Open-source, extensibility, contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Background
  - SOTA LLMs generate synthetic data; zero-shot generalization via fine-tuning without vast human annotation
  - models can evaluate / critique responses
  - models can refine: correct outputs given feedback
  - feedback mechanisms: human-in-the-loop, reward models, model-generated feedback
  - feedback forms: pairwise comparisons, scalar scores, natural language descriptions
  - refinement techniques: separate supervised refiners, domain-specific refinement
- Self-refinement
  - same LLM critiques and/or refines its own responses
  - smaller instruction-tuned models fail to replicate GPT-3.5 / GPT-4 refinement
  - without good stopping mechanisms, refining high-quality responses can make them worse
  - humans correct with objectives in mind = principles: faithfulness, specificity, safety (non-toxic), relevance; vary by task
  - goal: imbue these into conversational agents
- ProMiSe (Proxy Metric-based Self-Refinement)
  - iterative, principle-guided; for relatively smaller LMs
  - proxy metric thresholding per principle + principle-specific few-shot refinement + best-of-N rejection sampling
  - task-appropriate metrics, calibrated sufficiency thresholds, prompts suited to smaller models
  - multi-aspect via iterative single-aspect queries, not all dimensions at once
- Applications
  - content-grounded QA: consistent gains, single-turn
  - extended to multi-turn dialogue data generation (user queries + agent responses)
  - fine-tune llama-2-13b-chat on synthetic data: beats zero-shot baseline and models trained only on human annotations
- Extra points + contributions
  - open-source models, no black-box API; also works with closed-source
  - extendable to other tasks given proxy metrics + few in-context exemplars
  - contribution 1: domain-agnostic ProMiSe, in-context learning, proxy metrics as external feedback
  - contribution 2: MultiDoc2Dial, QuAC; 5 metrics (RougeL, Bert-Recall, Bert-K-Precision, Recall, K-Precision) + LLM-as-judge with GPT-4; few-shot + fine-tuning; release software + data
  - contribution 3: proxy metric change vs downstream metrics -> unsupervised correlation

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
State-of-the-art large language models (LLMs) have been shown to be good at generating new synthetic data, which helps improve zero-shot task generalization through fine-tuning without needing vast amounts of human annotations. Different approaches have been proposed showing that models can evaluate and critique responses, and also that they can refine, meaning they correct their outputs when given feedback. These works studied various feedback mechanisms (human-in-the-loop, reward models that capture human preferences, model-generated feedback) and forms of feedback (pairwise comparisons, scalar scores, natural language descriptions), and also refinement techniques (separate supervised refiners, domain-specific refinement).

Especially relevant are recent works on the self-refinement phenomenon, where the same LLM does critique and/or refinement on top of generating responses. These works show some shortcomings: smaller instruction-tuned models fail to replicate the refinement results of systems like GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, and without well-designed stopping mechanisms, self-refinement on high-quality responses can make the results worse. When humans correct themselves they often do it with one or more objectives in mind, i.e. principles. These principles can include faithfulness, specificity, safety (i.e. non-toxic), relevance to the question asked, etc., and they can be different across tasks. We want to put these aspects into conversational agents so that they show up in the agent's responses.

So we introduce an iterative, principle-guided approach to self-refinement in relatively smaller language models, where refinement has not worked before. Our algorithm is called Proxy Metric-based Self-Refinement (ProMiSe). It combines proxy metric thresholding for different principles with independent principle-specific few-shot refinement and best-of-N rejection sampling. This lets us deliberately select task-appropriate metrics with calibrated sufficiency thresholds, and use specific prompts that are designed to better match the instruction-following capabilities of smaller models. This way we do multi-aspect self-refinement through iterative single-aspect improvement queries, instead of refining on many dimensions at the same time.

- Applications
  - content-grounded QA: consistent gains on single-turn generation
  - multi-turn dialogue data generation (user queries + agent responses)
  - fine-tune llama-2-13b-chat on synthetic data: beats zero-shot baseline and human-annotation-only models
- Open-source models, no black-box API; also applies to closed-source; extendable with proxy metrics + few exemplars
- Contributions
  - domain-agnostic ProMiSe, in-context learning, proxy metrics as external feedback
  - MultiDoc2Dial, QuAC; 5 metrics (RougeL, Bert-Recall, Bert-K-Precision, Recall, K-Precision) + LLM-as-judge with GPT-4; release software + data
  - proxy metric change vs downstream metrics: unsupervised correlation

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
State-of-the-art large language models (LLMs) have been shown to be good at generating new synthetic data, which helps improve zero-shot task generalization through fine-tuning without needing vast amounts of human annotations. Different approaches have been proposed showing that models can evaluate and critique responses, and also that they can refine, meaning they correct their outputs when given feedback. These works studied various feedback mechanisms (human-in-the-loop, reward models that capture human preferences, model-generated feedback) and forms of feedback (pairwise comparisons, scalar scores, natural language descriptions), and also refinement techniques (separate supervised refiners, domain-specific refinement).

Especially relevant are recent works on the self-refinement phenomenon, where the same LLM does critique and/or refinement on top of generating responses. These works show some shortcomings: smaller instruction-tuned models fail to replicate the refinement results of systems like GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, and without well-designed stopping mechanisms, self-refinement on high-quality responses can make the results worse. When humans correct themselves they often do it with one or more objectives in mind, i.e. principles. These principles can include faithfulness, specificity, safety (i.e. non-toxic), relevance to the question asked, etc., and they can be different across tasks. We want to put these aspects into conversational agents so that they show up in the agent's responses.

So we introduce an iterative, principle-guided approach to self-refinement in relatively smaller language models, where refinement has not worked before. Our algorithm is called Proxy Metric-based Self-Refinement (ProMiSe). It combines proxy metric thresholding for different principles with independent principle-specific few-shot refinement and best-of-N rejection sampling. This lets us deliberately select task-appropriate metrics with calibrated sufficiency thresholds, and use specific prompts that are designed to better match the instruction-following capabilities of smaller models. This way we do multi-aspect self-refinement through iterative single-aspect improvement queries, instead of refining on many dimensions at the same time.

We apply the method to content-grounded question answering and show consistent improvements on a diverse set of evaluation metrics for single-turn response generation. Then we extend ProMiSe to multi-turn dialogue data generation, where it generates user queries as well as agent responses. We fine-tune llama-2-13b-chat on the synthetic data, and it improves significantly over the zero-shot baseline and over supervised models fine-tuned only on human annotations.

Importantly, this approach is built on open-source models and does not depend on proprietary models with black-box API access, but the algorithm can also be applied directly to closed-source models. It can also be extended to other tasks, as long as proxy metrics can be defined and a few in-context exemplars can be made for the relevant principles. Our key contributions are:

- We introduce a new domain-agnostic algorithm, ProMiSe, that does multi-aspect self-refinement on desirable principles for a response through in-context learning, with proxy metrics as external quality feedback.

- We apply ProMiSe to both content-grounded single-turn question answering and multi-turn dialogue generation. Extensive evaluations on MultiDoc2Dial and QuAC datasets with 5 automatic evaluation metrics (RougeL, Bert-Recall, Bert-K-Precision, Recall, K-Precision) and LLM-as-judge with GPT-4 show it is effective both in few-shot and fine-tuning settings. We will release the software and the synthetic dialogue data.

- We analyze the relationship between the change in proxy metric scores and the downstream evaluation metrics, which shows an unsupervised correlation and supports the efficacy of our method.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
State-of-the-art large language models (LLMs) have been shown to be effective in generating new synthetic data, which is useful for improving zero-shot task generalization through fine-tuning without requiring vast amounts of human annotations. Various approaches have shown the ability of models to evaluate and critique responses [1,2,3,4], as well as their potential to refine, i.e. to correct their outputs given feedback [5,6,7,8,9]. These explorations have studied various feedback mechanisms (human-in-the-loop, reward models capturing human preferences, model-generated feedback) and forms (pairwise comparisons, scalar scores, natural language descriptions), as well as refinement techniques (separate supervised refiners, domain-specific refinement).

Of particular note are recent works exploring the self-refinement phenomenon [7,9,3], which leverage the same LLM to perform critique and/or refinement on top of generating responses. These works reveal shortcomings: smaller instruction-tuned models fail to replicate the refinement results of systems such as GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, and in the absence of well-designed stopping mechanisms, self-refinement applied to high-quality responses can make the results worse [8]. When humans correct themselves, they often do so with one or more objectives, i.e. principles, in mind. Such principles may include faithfulness, specificity, safety (i.e. non-toxic), relevance to a question posed, etc., and may vary across tasks; we seek to imbue these aspects into conversational agents so that they are reflected in the agent's responses.

To this end, we introduce an iterative, principle-guided approach to self-refinement in relatively smaller language models, where refinement has previously proven unsuccessful. Our algorithm, Proxy Metric-based Self-Refinement (ProMiSe), combines proxy metric thresholding for different principles with independent principle-specific few-shot refinement and best-of-N rejection sampling. This allows for the deliberate selection of task-appropriate metrics with calibrated sufficiency thresholds, and of specific prompts designed to better match the instruction-following capabilities of smaller models. We thus perform multi-aspect self-refinement via iterative single-aspect improvement queries, as opposed to simultaneous refinement on many dimensions.

We apply this method to content-grounded question answering, demonstrating consistent improvements on a diverse set of evaluation metrics for single-turn response generation. We then extend ProMiSe to multi-turn dialogue data generation, generating user queries in addition to agent responses. Fine-tuning llama-2-13b-chat on the synthetic data yields significant improvement over the zero-shot baseline and over supervised models fine-tuned solely on human annotations.

Crucially, this approach is built on open-source models and does not rely on proprietary models with black-box API access, although the proposed algorithm can be directly applied to closed-source models as well. It can also be extended to other tasks, provided that proxy metrics can be defined and a few in-context exemplars can be created for the relevant principles. Our key contributions are:

- We introduce a novel domain-agnostic algorithm, ProMiSe, which performs multi-aspect self-refinement on desirable principles for a response through in-context learning, using proxy metrics as external quality feedback.

- We apply ProMiSe to both content-grounded single-turn question answering and multi-turn dialogue generation. Extensive evaluations on the MultiDoc2Dial and QuAC datasets with 5 automatic evaluation metrics (RougeL, Bert-Recall, Bert-K-Precision, Recall, K-Precision), as well as LLM-as-judge with GPT-4, demonstrate its effectiveness in both few-shot and fine-tuning settings. We will release both the software and the synthetic dialogue data.

- We analyze the relationship between the change in proxy metric scores and the downstream evaluation metrics, revealing an unsupervised correlation that reinforces the efficacy of our method.
